Pearl
purl
noun
Greek margaritēs (G3135), Hebrew gabish or peninim (H6443) — a precious organic gem formed within the shell of certain mollusks; uniquely in Scripture, the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem are EACH "of one pearl" (Rev 21:21), and the kingdom of heaven is compared to a merchant seeking a pearl of great price (Matt 13:45-46).

Biblical Definition

Pearl is one of the most theologically loaded gems in the New Testament. Christ used it twice: once in the parable of the pearl of great price (Matt 13:45-46) — the merchant who, finding one pearl of great price, sold all that he had and bought it, an icon of the disciple who counts the kingdom worth everything else combined; and once in the warning not to "cast your pearls before swine" (Matt 7:6) — a sober reminder that the holy things of God should not be flung before those who will only trample and tear. In Revelation, the New Jerusalem's twelve gates are each "of one pearl" (Rev 21:21) — a stunning detail, because pearls in nature are formed when an irritant (a grain of sand, a parasite) enters the oyster's shell and the oyster covers it with layer upon layer of nacre over years of suffering. The gates of the eternal city are the WOUNDED GATES — each formed by the response to an irritant, each the product of long suffering. This is the gospel built into the architecture of heaven: you enter the city of God only through gates formed by suffering — and the supreme suffering is that of the Lamb whose wounds purchased the city. The twelve gates also carry the names of the twelve tribes of Israel (Rev 21:12) — the people of God whose history of suffering and slow accretion of glory mirrors the pearl's formation. Pearl is the only ORGANIC gem in the biblical catalog (every other foundation stone is mineral); the city's gates are the LIVING produce of long covenant patience, and the entrance to glory is always through wounds borne by God Himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

An organic gem formed within mollusk shells; the parable of the kingdom's surpassing worth, and the material of the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem.

PEARL, noun. A smooth, rounded, white or pale-colored gem formed within the shell of certain mollusks (especially oysters) by layers of nacre (mother-of-pearl) deposited over years around an irritant.

In Scripture, the parable of the pearl of great price (Matt 13:45-46); the warning not to cast pearls before swine (Matt 7:6); the material of the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:21), each of "one pearl." The only organic substance in the biblical foundation-stone catalog.

Key Scripture

Matthew 13:45-46 — "Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it."

Revelation 21:21 — "And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass."

Matthew 7:6 — "Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you."

1 Timothy 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array."

Modern Corruption

Pearl is corrupted when the wound-formation symbolism is missed (treating the city's pearl gates as mere ornament rather than as suffering transfigured) or when the pearl of great price is read sentimentally instead of as the radical kingdom-cost theology Christ intended.

expand to see more

Wound-formation missed. The detail in Revelation 21:21 — that each of the twelve gates is ONE pearl — is staggering when you consider how pearls form. An oyster covers an irritant with layers of nacre over years; the larger the pearl, the longer the suffering. The gates of the city of God are produced through patient endurance of wound. This is gospel architecture: the entrance to the eternal city is through gates that bear in their very substance the long story of suffering transfigured into beauty. Christ's wounds purchased the city; the saints' wounds patterned the gates. To strip this is to strip the city of its suffering-formed glory.

Sentimental pearl-of-great-price. The parable of the merchant who sells all to buy one pearl is sometimes treated as a touching story about Jesus' love for sinners (Jesus is the merchant; we are the pearl). This inversion misses Christ's intended meaning: the kingdom IS the pearl; the disciple IS the merchant; and the disciple's response should be radical liquidation of everything else to obtain it. The kingdom costs you everything; it is worth everything. Soft-pedaling this empties the parable of its discipleship demand.

"Each gate of the eternal city is one pearl — wounds transfigured into glory, suffering layered into the entrance of heaven."
